concentration-time-s1.title: Cyclopropane turning into propene
concentration-time-s1.text:
When heated to a fixed high temperature, cyclopropane gas rearranges into propene:

C₃H₆ (cyclopropane) → C₃H₆ (propene)

A student records [cyclopropane] over time and calculates two more columns from it.

table.caption: Concentration of cyclopropane over time, with ln[C₃H₆] and 1/[C₃H₆]

concentration-time-s2.title: Nitrogen dioxide breaking down
concentration-time-s2.text: At a fixed high temperature, nitrogen dioxide decomposes: 2 NO₂(g) → 2 NO(g) + O₂(g). A student measures [NO₂] and plots 1/[NO₂] against time.

concentration-time-s3.title: Ammonia on a hot metal wire
concentration-time-s3.text: Ammonia gas breaks down on the surface of a hot tungsten wire: 2 NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g). The graph shows [NH₃] against time.

items.q: Which claim about the order of this reaction is best supported by the table?
options: First order: ln[C₃H₆] drops about 0.30 per 500 s
Second order: 1/[C₃H₆] goes up in each 500 s interval
Zero order: [C₃H₆] goes down in each 500 s interval
First order, because the graph of these data is linear

why.correct: ln[C₃H₆] goes −3.00, −3.30, −3.60, −3.90, −4.19: it falls by about 0.30 each 500 s, so a plot of ln[C₃H₆] against time is a straight line, which means first order. 1/[C₃H₆] rises by more each interval (20.0, 27.0, 36.5, 49.3, 66.2), so that plot curves.
options: Right: equal steps in ln[A] in equal times means ln[A] vs t is linear, which is first order.
1/[A] rises, but by growing amounts (not equal steps), so 1/[A] vs t is not linear; it is not second order.
[A] falls by shrinking amounts (0.0130, 0.0096, ...), so [A] vs t is curved; it is not zero order.
This is the claim readers do not accept: it does not say which graph is linear. Name the plot, ln[A] against time.

items.q: Use the first and last rows to find the rate constant k. Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you used log (base 10). The integrated rate law uses the natural log, ln.
Value: that slope comes from the 1/[A] column, the second-order plot. This reaction is first order, so use the ln[A] column.

why.correct: For first order, ln[A] vs t has slope −k. k = −(ln[A]₂₀₀₀ − ln[A]₀)/(2000 s − 0 s) = −(−4.19 − (−3.00))/2000 s = 1.19/2000 s = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.

items.q: With k = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, what is the half-life of cyclopropane at this temperature? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied. The half-life is t½ = 0.693 / k.
Value: t½ = 0.693/k; you left out the 0.693 (that is ln 2).

why.correct: t½ = 0.693 / k = 0.693 / (6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) = 1155 s, which is 1.2 × 10³ s to two significant figures. Check with the table: [C₃H₆] falls from 0.0500 M to 0.0250 M somewhere between 1000 s and 1500 s.

items.q: Predict [C₃H₆], in M, at 3000 s if the reaction continues the same way.

mistakes.why: Value: that is ln[A], not [A]. Finish by taking e to that power: [A] = e^(ln[A]).
Value: you used 10^(−kt). The first-order law uses e^(−kt) (natural log).

items.q: Which statement correctly uses the graph to find the order with respect to NO₂?
options: 1/[NO₂] vs time is linear, so second order
The plot is a straight line, so the reaction is zero order in NO₂
1/[NO₂] vs time is linear, so the reaction is first order in NO₂
The plot rises, so [NO₂] rises with time and NO₂ is a product here

why.correct: A straight line for 1/[A] against time is the signature of second order (1/[A]t = kt + 1/[A]₀). The justification names the plot that is linear.
options: Right: names the linear plot and draws the right conclusion.
Zero order would make [NO₂] against time linear, not 1/[NO₂].
First order would make ln[NO₂] against time linear.
1/[NO₂] rises because [NO₂] falls; NO₂ is the reactant.

items.q: Use the slope of the 1/[NO₂] line to find the second-order rate constant. Include units.

mistakes.why: Sign: for second order the slope of 1/[A] vs t is +k, and k is positive.
Value: read two points from the line and divide the rise by the run: (75 − 25) M⁻¹ ÷ 100 s.

why.correct: For second order, slope of 1/[A] vs t = k. Slope = (75 M⁻¹ − 25 M⁻¹)/(100 s − 0 s) = 0.50 M⁻¹ s⁻¹.

items.q: How long, in seconds, does it take for [NO₂] to fall from 0.0400 M to 0.0100 M?

mistakes.why: Value: you used the first-order half-life twice. This is second order: use 1/[A]t − 1/[A]₀ = kt.
Value: you multiplied by k. Solve for t: t = (1/[A]t − 1/[A]₀)/k.

items.q: How does the time for [NO₂] to halve change as the reaction goes on?
options: It gets longer, since the rate falls with [NO₂]²
It stays the same, since half-lives are constant for any reaction
It gets shorter, since there is less NO₂ left to react each time
It stays the same, since the rate constant k does not change

why.correct: From 0.0400 to 0.0200 M: (50 − 25)/0.50 = 50 s. From 0.0200 to 0.0100 M: (100 − 50)/0.50 = 100 s. For second order the halving time doubles each time, because the rate falls with the square of the concentration.
options: Right: 50 s, then 100 s.
A constant half-life belongs to first-order reactions only.
Less reactant means a slower rate, so halving takes longer, not shorter.
k is constant, but for second order the half-life also depends on [A].

items.q: What is the order of this reaction with respect to NH₃, and what is the evidence?
options: Zero order: [NH₃] vs time is a straight line
First order: [NH₃] falls steadily with time
Second order: [NH₃] vs time slopes downward
Zero order: the rate drops to zero by the end

why.correct: [NH₃] against time is linear, so the rate (the slope) is the same at every concentration: zero order. For first or second order, [A] against time curves.
options: Right: the linear plot named is [A] vs t, which is zero order.
A first-order reaction gives a curve for [A] vs t; ln[A] vs t would be the straight one.
A second-order reaction gives a curve for [A] vs t; 1/[A] vs t would be the straight one.
The rate is constant until the NH₃ runs out; that is why the line is straight.

items.q: What is the rate constant k, from the slope of the line? Include units.

mistakes.why: Sign: the slope of [A] vs t is −k; k itself is positive.
Value: for zero order, k is the slope itself, not the slope divided by [A].

why.correct: Slope = (0.0000 M − 0.0200 M)/(80 s − 0 s) = −2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s. For zero order, slope = −k, so k = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.

items.q: While [NH₃] falls at 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, at what rate does H₂ form, in M/s?

mistakes.why: Value: H₂ has a different coefficient. 3 H₂ form for every 2 NH₃ used, so multiply by 3/2.
Value: the ratio is inverted. H₂ (coefficient 3) forms faster than NH₃ (coefficient 2) is used.

why.correct: Δ[H₂]/Δt = (3/2)(2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s) = 3.75 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, which is 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ M/s to two significant figures.

items.q: The wire's surface has a fixed number of spots where NH₃ can sit and react. Which explanation of the zero-order behavior fits this?
options: The spots stay full, so a fixed number react per second
NH₃ molecules in the gas react with each other, away from the wire
The wire itself is used up at a steady rate, and that sets the rate
The NH₃ molecules in the gas react at the same instant

why.correct: When every spot on the surface is occupied, adding more NH₃ to the gas cannot speed things up: the number of reacting molecules per second is set by the surface, so the rate does not depend on [NH₃].
options: Right: a saturated surface makes the rate independent of the gas concentration.
If NH₃ molecules reacted with each other in the gas, the rate would depend on [NH₃].
The wire is not a reactant in 2 NH₃ → N₂ + 3 H₂.
If everything reacted at once, the concentration would drop to zero at once, not along a line.

items.q: Iodine-131 decays by a first-order process with a half-life of 8.02 days. How many days pass until 12.5% of a sample is left?

mistakes.why: Value: two half-lives leave 25%. 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% is three half-lives.
Value: 12.5% is (½)³, so three half-lives, not eight.

why.correct: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% is three half-lives: 3 × 8.02 days = 24.1 days. Radioactive decay is first order, so every half-life is the same length.

items.q: A first-order reaction is run twice at the same temperature, the second time with twice the starting concentration. Predict each change in the second run.

variables.name: Initial rate
variables.why: rate = k[A], so doubling [A] doubles the initial rate.

variables.name: Half-life
variables.why: For first order t½ = 0.693/k, which does not depend on concentration.

variables.name: Rate constant k
variables.why: k depends on temperature, which is unchanged.

variables.name: Slope of ln[A] against time
variables.why: The slope is −k, and k is unchanged; the line just starts higher.

why.correct: Doubling [A]₀ doubles the rate, but k, the half-life and the slope of the ln[A] plot all stay the same.

items.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0350 min⁻¹. Starting at 0.800 M, what is [A] after 20.0 min, in M?

mistakes.why: Value: you used base 10. The first-order law is [A]t = [A]₀e^(−kt).
Value: that subtracts kt as if the reaction were zero order.

items.q: Which pair correctly matches a straight-line plot with its slope?
options: ln[A] vs t, first order; slope −k
1/[A] vs t, second order; slope −k
[A] vs t, first order; slope −k
ln[A] vs t, second order; slope +k

why.correct: First order: ln[A] vs t, slope −k. Second order: 1/[A] vs t, slope +k. Zero order: [A] vs t, slope −k.
options: Right: the first-order plot falls with slope −k.
1/[A] rises over time, so its slope is +k, not −k.
For first order, [A] vs t curves; only ln[A] vs t is straight.
ln[A] vs t is the first-order plot, and it falls.

items.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 45 s. What is k, in s⁻¹?

mistakes.why: Value: rearrange t½ = 0.693/k to k = 0.693/t½, not t½/0.693.
Value: k = 0.693/t½; you left out ln 2 = 0.693.

why.correct: k = 0.693 / t½ = 0.693 / 45 s = 0.0154 s⁻¹, which is 0.015 s⁻¹ to two significant figures.
